effect.text: 26 January 1788: the First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove and the colony of New South Wales is proclaimed.
More transports arrive from Britain, bearing convict labour for the young colony.
Merino sheep are landed — the colony's wool prospects rise.
The merino flock is left to graze; its promise will keep.
A harsh drought settles over the colony; the ground cracks and the crops wither.
Bushfires sweep through the district, driven by a hot northerly wind.
The Hawkesbury bursts its banks and the floodwaters take the season's grain.
A bountiful season — the granaries fill and spirits lift.
A shore whaling station opens; oil and bone fetch a fine price in London.
Free settlers step ashore, seeking land and a new start.
The colony rallies to help the new arrivals find their feet.
A party of convicts absconds into the bush; the guard is turned out to recapture them.
Rather than pursue the absconders, the governor offers emancipation to those who return and work.
The transportation of convicts to the eastern colonies ends; the settlements turn to free labour and self-government.
Squatters take up vast pastoral runs far beyond the settled districts; the wool clip swells.
The government issues depasturing licences to bring the squatters' runs under order.
Colonial merino fleece commands high prices on the London wool market; the clip ships out at a handsome return.
An expedition sets out to cross the interior; much country is charted, though the arid centre exacts a heavy toll.
The colony judges the interior crossing too costly and holds the expedition back for now.
Gold is struck at Bathurst, then Ballarat and Bendigo; the rush is on, and diggers pour onto the fields.
A rich payable field is opened near the settlement; the crushers run day and night.
Shiploads of new arrivals land for the diggings; the colonial population swells.
After the Eureka Stockade at Ballarat, the licence is abolished for the miner's right and the vote; the goldfields win a measure of democracy.
The troops storm the stockade at Ballarat; order is restored, but at a cost in blood and standing.
Bushrangers hold up the gold escort on the road from the diggings and make off with the consignment.
The first railway and telegraph lines open in the colonies; passengers, freight, and news begin to move at a new pace.
The Overland Telegraph is completed from Adelaide to Darwin and joined to the submarine cable; the colonies now reach London in hours, not months.
A vast silver-lead lode is proved at Broken Hill; the mines and smelters make fortunes and a new mining colony.
The first frozen meat cargoes reach London in good order; refrigeration opens the British market to colonial beef and mutton.
A new trunk railway links the colonies further, though the differing gauges force a change of train at the border.
The colony defers the costly railway extension for another session of parliament.
Speculation and easy credit make 'Marvellous Melbourne' one of the richest cities in the world; land values soar.
The land boom collapses and a run on the banks in 1893 closes many of them; depositors are ruined and the colonies fall into depression.
The Great Shearers' Strike ends in a settlement; out of the shearers' unions grows a labour movement and, in time, a Labor party.
The strike is broken with non-union labour and mounted police; the clip comes in, but bitterness lingers on the runs.
South Australia grants women the vote and the right to stand for parliament — the first Australian colony to do so, and among the first in the world.
Delegates from the colonies meet in convention and draft a constitution for a federal Commonwealth of Australia.
At referendum the colonies vote to approve the constitution and join the Commonwealth; the people carry Federation.
A first referendum falls short of the quota; the constitution is amended and put to the people again.
The Federation Drought grips the continent; the rivers fall to a trickle and stock perish in their millions across the inland.
